_sources.title: Urban heat islands and surface temperatures
Urban heat islands and surface temperatures

1.why: Concrete has a smaller specific heat than water, so the same energy warms it more.

wrong.a: Water has a big c, so it warms slowly.
wrong.c: Wet soil holds water, which slows warming.
wrong.d: Sea water has a big c, like all water.

2.why: ΔT is the change in temperature resulting from added heat energy.

wrong.b: Time is represented by t, not ΔT.
wrong.c: Thickness is not part of this equation.
wrong.d: Total energy is represented by Q.

3.why: Trees provide shade and evaporate water, which removes heat from the air.

wrong.a: Dark roofs absorb more solar energy.
wrong.b: Car parks store massive amounts of heat.
wrong.d: Windows do not change heat storage.

_quiz_pool.question: What does c stand for in Q = m × c × ΔT?
_quiz_pool.explanation: c tells how much energy 1 kg needs to warm by 1 °C.

_quiz_pool.question: Which warms fastest with the same energy?
_quiz_pool.explanation: Concrete has a smaller c than water, so its temperature rises more.

_quiz_pool.question: What is the unit of energy Q?
If you double the mass, the energy needed for the same ΔT…
_quiz_pool.explanation: Q grows in step with m.

_quiz_pool.question: Why do parks feel cooler than car parks?
options: Plants and water store heat and evaporate water
_quiz_pool.explanation: Water has a big c and evaporation takes heat away.

safety: no flame, no kettle, no mains electricity

cover.title: Why city streets get so hot
cover.subtitle: Roads and roofs soak up sunlight all day. Find out why concrete warms faster than water, and how a city stays hot at night.
cover.subject: Physics · Heat
cover.fun_fact: Water needs almost 5 times more energy than concrete to warm up by the same amount.
story.title: A hot week in the city
story.lead: Weather records note high daytime temperatures across Jakarta [1]. Streets and concrete roofs absorb intense sunlight, warming up much faster than green parks [2].
story.image_caption: City surfaces and rooftop temperatures mapped from space
stat.1.label: degrees Fahrenheit reached in spring 2026 [2]
stat.2.label: September date of late heat records [2]
stat.3.label: minute read on NASA heat observations [2]
story.body_1: A city has many dark roads and concrete structures that soak in solar radiation all day. After sunset, this stored thermal energy slowly radiates outward [2]. This keeps urban nights warmer than rural areas, forming an urban heat island.
story.body_2: High temperatures affect daily comfort and health, especially for children [3]. Planting trees and installing reflective roofs help reduce heat storage by providing shade and cooling through evaporation [2].
timeline.1.text: Sunlight begins heating dark roofs and pavement.
timeline.2.text: Concrete surfaces reach peak temperatures well above ambient air.
timeline.3.text: Stored heat radiates slowly into the night air.
physics.title: Heat, mass and temperature
physics.body_1: Adding energy raises the temperature of an object. The temperature rise depends on mass, material type, and the amount of thermal energy transferred.
physics.body_2: Every substance has a specific heat capacity, c. Materials with a small c heat up rapidly when energy is applied. Water has a large c, so it warms up slowly.
physics.assumptions: We assume no heat is lost to the surrounding air during energy transfer.

lab.title: Sun test: soil vs water
lab.step_1: Fill one cup with water and another with dry soil or sand.
lab.step_2: Place both cups side by side in direct sunlight for 20 minutes.
lab.step_3: Touch each cup or measure temperature to see which is hotter.
lab.question: Which cup became hotter? Use specific heat capacity to explain.
